name: Ajrakh resist block printing (Kutch Ajrakh)

region.place: Ajrakhpur (also Dhamadka and Khavda); related practice in Barmer (Rajasthan) and Sindh (Pakistan)

summary: Ajrakh is a resist- and mordant-dyed, hand block-printed cotton textile made by Khatri printers whose ancestors came from Sindh; in India it is centred at Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda in Kutch, with related practice in Barmer. Its 14-16 stage sequence combines lime-gum and mud resists, iron-black and alum mordant printing, indigo vat dyeing and madder or alizarin red dyeing, traditionally in a four-colour palette and often printed identically on both sides. After the 2001 earthquake and deteriorating water at Dhamadka, printers founded Ajrakhpur; the craft was registered as the 'Kutch Ajrakh' GI (application 1050) in 2024.

concepts.title: Kutch Ajrakh (Ajrakh resist block printing)
concepts.summary: Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique involving a series of direct and resist printing and dyeing steps.
concepts.body_md:
Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique involving a series of direct and resist printing and dyeing steps. [S1]

Traditionally four colours are used (blue, black, red, white) and a piece needs all four to be called ajrakh. [S1]

The process and designs of Ajrakh printing are common to Sindh, Kutch and Barmer district of Rajasthan (1971 Kutch District Gazetteer as quoted in the GI journal). [S1]

V&A labels describe ajrakh as a laborious technique from western Rajasthan, Kutch and Sindh. [S4]

Ajrakh is printed by Khatri artisans; Dhamadka and Khavda in Kutch became main centres, followed by Barmer. [S6]

Kutch Ajrakh was filed as GI application 1050 on 31-01-2023 by Ajarakhpur Hastkala Vikas Sangathan, advertised in GI Journal 188, and registered (certificate dated 22-04-2024). [S1, S2]

concepts.title: Sindh and Indus-region origins
concepts.summary: Ajrakh printing originally came from Sindh (1971 Gazetteer, quoted in GI journal).
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh printing originally came from Sindh (1971 Gazetteer, quoted in GI journal). [S1]

The GI text argues block printing on cotton in India is thought to be over 4500 years old, citing Indus Valley geometric patterning and dye technology. [S1]

Khamir reports 3000-year-old madder-dyed cotton strands found at an ancient dyer's workshop in Mohenjo-Daro; it does not tie these finds directly to the Khatris. [S7]

The likely origins of Ajrakh lie in Sind. [S12]

19th-century ajrakh cloths made in Sind are held by the V&A (e.g. 5473A/(IS), ca. 1855-79). [S4]

concepts.title: Khatri migration from Sindh to Kutch
concepts.summary: The technique came to Kutch from Sindh some 400 years ago at the behest of the King of Kutch, who invited Khatri craftsmen to the banks of the Dhamadka river.
concepts.body_md:
The technique came to Kutch from Sindh some 400 years ago at the behest of the King of Kutch, who invited Khatri craftsmen to the banks of the Dhamadka river. [S1]

Rao Bharmalji I (1586-1631) invited Khatri printers from Sindh and gave them land and tax exemptions. [S6]

An artisan account says Rao Barmalji I invited Sindhi artisans, offering land, housing and tax exemptions. [S7]

Khamir's account says Hindu Khatris fled Sindh to Kachchh in the 7th century after Arab invasion; Ajrakhpur and Dhamadka Khatris trace their line to Jinda Jeeva, said to have arrived around 1650. [S7]

A legend links the craft to Dhamadka following a 16th-century migration. [S12]

concepts.title: Dhamadka as the historic centre
concepts.summary: Ajrakh activities prevailed at Dhamadka for the past 450 years because of a water source from a stream of the Indus river; this stream dried up in 1989.
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh activities prevailed at Dhamadka for the past 450 years because of a water source from a stream of the Indus river; this stream dried up in 1989. [S1]

The Dhamadka river was the only one in Kutch said to flow in the opposite direction, emptying into the Banni rather than flowing south; the rangchulis were around the old river. [S1]

The river Saran in Dhamadka dried up by 1989, largely because bore pumps diverted water toward the Kandla Free Trade Zone. [S9]

Khatri families settled near the Saran river, where they washed their fabric. [S14]

Dhamadka is located approximately 50 km east of Bhuj (GI); a Gaatha page gives almost 30 km. [S1, S14]

concepts.title: 2001 earthquake and founding of Ajrakhpur
concepts.summary: After a massive earthquake in 2001 the block printers were forced to relocate and settled in Ajrakhpur; over 100 families live there with 30 official workshops.
concepts.body_md:
After a massive earthquake in 2001 the block printers were forced to relocate and settled in Ajrakhpur; over 100 families live there with 30 official workshops. [S1]

Dhamadka was completely destroyed in the 2001 earthquake; printers bought land about 40 km away and founded Ajrakhpur, chosen for its good water source; it has about 80 Khatri families. [S9]

After the 2001 quake groundwater quality worsened in Dhamadka and about 100 families moved about 40 km to Ajrakhpur. [S10]

Artisans established Ajrakhpur with government and social support after the earthquake damaged Dhamadka. [S6]

concepts.title: Maldhari pastoralist clientele and traditional use
concepts.summary: The fabric was traditionally worn by members of the royal court and the pastoral Maldhari community; men used it as cummerbunds, lungis, turbans and shoulder cloths.
concepts.body_md:
The fabric was traditionally worn by members of the royal court and the pastoral Maldhari community; men used it as cummerbunds, lungis, turbans and shoulder cloths. [S1]

Maldharis also used the cloth as bundles to carry belongings while travelling. [S1]

Khatris made cloth for Maldharis and farming communities, often trading cloth for produce, milk or ghee; designs were not interchangeable between communities. [S7]

Traditional buyers include Maldharis in Kutch, Muslim Patels in Marwar and Muslim potters in Barmer. [S6]

concepts.title: Shift to synthetic dyes and natural-dye revival
concepts.summary: Alizarin, synthesised in 1868, rapidly superseded madder; madder use almost disappeared and is now being revived.
concepts.body_md:
Alizarin, synthesised in 1868, rapidly superseded madder; madder use almost disappeared and is now being revived. [S1]

Synthetic dyes replaced most natural colour in the Indian market in the early 1950s; interest in traditional craft revived in the 1970s. [S8]

In the mid-2010s most block printers worked with chemical dyes; some printers serve both natural and chemical dye markets according to demand. [S9]

Globalisation is changing Ajrakh techniques, designs, materials and markets. [S12]

concepts.title: Iron content of process water
concepts.summary: Presence of iron in the water supply dulls and darkens the final result; alum, tin or chrome deposits help brighten colours.
concepts.body_md:
Presence of iron in the water supply dulls and darkens the final result; alum, tin or chrome deposits help brighten colours. [S1]

Iron content in the water increased drastically after the earthquake, making prints black so that off-white backgrounds were not possible. [S9]

An artisan reports that even small amounts of iron cause black spots on the pale yellow (harde-treated) cloth, and that a family test of Dhamadka groundwater found high iron. [S10]

Excess iron in groundwater threatened Ajrakh in Dhamadka and is again threatening it in Ajrakhpur. [S10]

concepts.title: Water availability and falling water tables
concepts.summary: Ajrakh is described as a 16-stage, water-intensive technique; an artisan states that the craftsmen's requirement is to recycle about 1 lakh litres of water every day.
concepts.body_md:
Ajrakh is described as a 16-stage, water-intensive technique; an artisan states that the craftsmen's requirement is to recycle about 1 lakh litres of water every day. [S10]

In 2019 a CETP was being set up through NITRA, with an iron filter and dual media filter so process water could be reused. [S10]

A government-funded effluent treatment system was built in Ajrakhpur in 2022, with recycled water reusable for washing fabric. [S11]

Water levels have been going down by 10-15 feet every year; no comprehensive water management plan has emerged. [S9]

Water is an important ingredient in getting the right colour; quality matters as much as quantity. [S1]
